title: Everyone pays $5. Is it worth $5 to all?
hook: Five buyers, one price. Who gets more than they paid for?

knows: that a market has one price for everyone
that buyers differ in how much they would pay
doesNotKnow: that most buyers get more value than they pay, and the gap can be added up

misconception: At the market price, everyone is paying exactly what it is worth to them.
objective: The learner can explain that each buyer who values a good above its price keeps the difference, and add those gaps: at $5, buyers worth $10, $8, $6 keep $5 + $3 + $1 = $9.

claims.text: At a $5 price, three of the five buyers ($10, $8, $6) buy; the $4 and $2 buyers stay out.
claims.source: A buyer buys when the cup is worth at least the price: 10, 8, 6 ≥ 5; 4, 2 < 5. Demo.tsx buys().

claims.text: Together they pay $15, value the cups at $24, and keep $5 + $3 + $1 = $9.
At other prices on the slider the same rule applies, e.g. at $3 four buy and keep 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = $16.
claims.source: gain(v, p) = v − p for v ≥ p. The stage total counts only buyers the learner has tapped.

claims.text: The total of what buyers keep (worth minus price) is called consumer surplus.
claims.source: Standard definition, e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 7 (consumers, producers and the efficiency of markets), which uses the same buyers-with-values construction.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: five invented buyers, one cup each, one price for everyone.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: five invented buyers, one cup each'.

recall.question: A concert sells every ticket at $40. One fan would have paid $100, another exactly $40. What is true?
options: Both got exactly what they paid for
The first fan kept $60 of value; the second kept nothing
recall.why: Each buyer keeps the gap between what the ticket is worth to them and the price: $100 − $40 = $60 for the first, $0 for the second.
